claim: TRIM32 is a member of the Tripartite motif (TRIM)-containing family of proteins defined by an N-terminal RING domain, one or two B-boxes, a coiled-coil domain, and a variable C-terminal region.
source: This protein is a member of the Tripartite motif (TRIM)-containing family of proteins defined by an N-terminal RING domain, one or two B-boxes, a coiled-coil domain, and a variable C-terminal region (Tocchini and Ciosk, 2015; Watanabe and Hatakeyama, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Tocchini and Ciosk, 2015; Watanabe and Hatakeyama, 2017).

claim: In TRIM32, six Ncl-1, HT2A, Lin-41 (NHL) repeats comprise the C-terminus.
source: In TRIM32, six Ncl-1, HT2A, Lin-41 (NHL) repeats comprise the C-terminus and are proposed to mediate the diverse functions of TRIM32, including cell proliferation, neuronal differentiation, muscle physiology and regeneration, and tumorigenesis (Lazzari and Meroni, 2016; Tocchini and Ciosk, 2015; Watanabe and Hatakeyama, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Lazzari and Meroni, 2016; Tocchini and Ciosk, 2015; Watanabe and Hatakeyama, 2017).

claim: The NHL repeats in TRIM32 are proposed to mediate diverse functions including cell proliferation, neuronal differentiation, muscle physiology and regeneration, and tumorigenesis.
source: In TRIM32, six Ncl-1, HT2A, Lin-41 (NHL) repeats comprise the C-terminus and are proposed to mediate the diverse functions of TRIM32, including cell proliferation, neuronal differentiation, muscle physiology and regeneration, and tumorigenesis (Lazzari and Meroni, 2016; Tocchini and Ciosk, 2015; Watanabe and Hatakeyama, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Lazzari and Meroni, 2016; Tocchini and Ciosk, 2015; Watanabe and Hatakeyama, 2017).

claim: A single mutation in the B-box region of TRIM32 causes Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS).
source: A single mutation in the B-box region of TRIM32 causes the multisystemic disorder Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) (Chiang et al., 2006), while multiple mutations that cluster in the NHL domains result in the muscle disorders Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2H (LGMD2H) and Sarcotubular Myopathy (STM) (Borg et al., 2009; Frosk et al., 2005; Lazzari et al., 2019; Nectoux et al., 2015; Neri et al., 2013; Schoser et al., 2005; Servián-Morilla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Chiang et al., 2006).

claim: Multiple mutations that cluster in the NHL domains of TRIM32 result in Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2H (LGMD2H) and Sarcotubular Myopathy (STM).
source: A single mutation in the B-box region of TRIM32 causes the multisystemic disorder Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) (Chiang et al., 2006), while multiple mutations that cluster in the NHL domains result in the muscle disorders Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2H (LGMD2H) and Sarcotubular Myopathy (STM) (Borg et al., 2009; Frosk et al., 2005; Lazzari et al., 2019; Nectoux et al., 2015; Neri et al., 2013; Schoser et al., 2005; Servián-Morilla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Borg et al., 2009; Frosk et al., 2005; Lazzari et al., 2019; Nectoux et al., 2015; Neri et al., 2013; Schoser et al., 2005; Servián-Morilla et al., 2019).

claim: Causative mutations in human LGMD2H cluster in the NHL repeats of TRIM32.
source: Causative mutations in human LGMD2H cluster in the NHL repeats (Figure 1A; Borg et al., 2009; Cossée et al., 2009; Frosk et al., 2005; Lazzari et al., 2019; Nectoux et al., 2015; Neri et al., 2013; Schoser et al., 2005), suggesting that this region may mediate protein-protein interactions important in disease prevention.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Borg et al., 2009; Cossée et al., 2009; Frosk et al., 2005; Lazzari et al., 2019; Nectoux et al., 2015; Neri et al., 2013; Schoser et al., 2005) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Mutations in Drosophila TRIM32 show progressive larval muscle degeneration.
source: We previously showed that mutations in Drosophila TRIM32 also show progressive larval muscle degeneration, despite modest sequence identity (~42%) across the NHL domains (LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).

claim: Drosophila TRIM32 has modest sequence identity (~42%) across the NHL domains compared to mammalian TRIM32.
source: We previously showed that mutations in Drosophila TRIM32 also show progressive larval muscle degeneration, despite modest sequence identity (~42%) across the NHL domains (LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).

claim: A crystal structure of Drosophila TRIM32_NHL was obtained at 2.6 Å resolution.
source: To gain molecular-level insight into the functional conservation between the NHL regions in fly and mammalian TRIM32, we obtained a crystal structure of TRIM32_NHL at 2.6 Å resolution (Rwork/Rfree = 18.2/22.8%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (crystallography) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The TRIM32_NHL structure features a six-bladed β-propeller, where each NHL repeat is comprised of four antiparallel β-strands.
source: This structure features a six-bladed β-propeller, where each NHL repeat is comprised of four antiparallel β-strands (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data and reference to Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The NHL region of Drosophila TRIM32 is a faithful model to understand NHL function in mouse TRIM32.
source: Indeed, the superimposition of these two structures demonstrate that the NHL region of Drosophila TRIM32 is a faithful model to understand NHL function (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison data and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Tropomyosin (Tm) and Troponin T (TnT) co-purify with TRIM32_NHL in mass spectrometry analysis.
source: In addition to the recovery of our bait protein, we detected peptides corresponding to Tropomyosin (Tm) and Troponin T (TnT) (Figure 1—source data 2), which are both known polyubiquitinated substrates of mammalian TRIM32 (Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1—source data 2) and citation to published literature (Cohen et al., 2012).

claim: Tropomyosin and Troponin T are known polyubiquitinated substrates of mammalian TRIM32.
source: In addition to the recovery of our bait protein, we detected peptides corresponding to Tropomyosin (Tm) and Troponin T (TnT) (Figure 1—source data 2), which are both known polyubiquitinated substrates of mammalian TRIM32 (Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Cohen et al., 2012).

claim: Glycolytic enzymes were enriched in the list of possible NHL-binding proteins from mass spectrometry analysis.
source: Surprisingly, glycolytic enzymes were also enriched in the list of possible NHL-binding proteins (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 2) and were further evaluated for physical interactions with TRIM32.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 2).

claim: Tropomyosin 2 (Tm2) physically interacts with TRIM32_NHL in vitro.
source: Indeed, incubation of TRIM32_NHL together with His-tagged Tm2 confirmed a physical interaction between these two proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Aldolase (Ald) directly interacts with the NHL domains of TRIM32 in vitro.
source: Both Ald and Pglym were found to directly interact with the NHL domains of TRIM32 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data (Figure 2A,B).

claim: Phosphoglycerate mutase 78 (Pglym) directly interacts with the NHL domains of TRIM32 in vitro.
source: Both Ald and Pglym were found to directly interact with the NHL domains of TRIM32 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data (Figure 2A,B).

claim: No binding was detected between TRIM32_NHL and the His-tagged control protein SCIN.
source: Note that no binding was detected between TRIM32_NHL and the His-tagged control protein SCIN, ruling out non-specific binding of the His tag.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data.

claim: Tropomyosin co-immunoprecipitates with full-length TRIM32 in vivo.
source: As expected, immunoprecipitation of TRIM32 successfully pulled-down Tm as an interacting protein at the predicted molecular weight of ~37 kD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Aldolase co-immunoprecipitates with full-length TRIM32 in vivo.
source: We also confirmed that both Ald and Pglym co-immunoprecipitate with anti-TRIM32 antibody.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 2C,D).

claim: Phosphoglycerate mutase co-immunoprecipitates with full-length TRIM32 in vivo.
source: We also confirmed that both Ald and Pglym co-immunoprecipitate with anti-TRIM32 antibody.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 2C,D).

claim: Aldolase and Pglym migrate at a higher molecular weight than expected in immunoprecipitation experiments, suggestive of post-translational modification.
source: Interestingly, the bands corresponding to these proteins migrated at a higher molecular weight than the expected size present in input lysates (Figure 2C,D; asterisk), suggestive of a post-translational modification.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 2C,D) and inference from molecular weight differences.

claim: Mutations in tn reduce Aldolase protein levels by approximately 50% in L3 larvae.
source: Strikingly, this same loss of TRIM32 resulted in a ~ 50% decrease in the protein levels of Ald or Pglym78 (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data (Figure 2E,F).

claim: Mutations in tn reduce Pglym protein levels by approximately 50% in L3 larvae.
source: Strikingly, this same loss of TRIM32 resulted in a ~ 50% decrease in the protein levels of Ald or Pglym78 (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data (Figure 2E,F).

claim: The downregulation of Ald and Pglym protein levels in tn mutants is not due to decreased transcription.
source: This downregulation was not due to a decrease in TRIM32-mediated transcription as mRNA levels of Ald or Pglym were not altered in tn-/- (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 results in decreased pyruvate levels in L3 larvae.
source: Examination of individual metabolites upon loss of TRIM32 showed a decrease in the terminal glycolytic products pyruvate and lactate as well as significant depletion of the glucose-derived metabolites glycerol-3-phosphate and 2-hydroxyglutarate (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3A,B).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 results in decreased lactate levels in L3 larvae.
source: Examination of individual metabolites upon loss of TRIM32 showed a decrease in the terminal glycolytic products pyruvate and lactate as well as significant depletion of the glucose-derived metabolites glycerol-3-phosphate and 2-hydroxyglutarate (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3A,B).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 results in significant depletion of glycerol-3-phosphate in L3 larvae.
source: Examination of individual metabolites upon loss of TRIM32 showed a decrease in the terminal glycolytic products pyruvate and lactate as well as significant depletion of the glucose-derived metabolites glycerol-3-phosphate and 2-hydroxyglutarate (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3A,B).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 results in significant depletion of 2-hydroxyglutarate in L3 larvae.
source: Examination of individual metabolites upon loss of TRIM32 showed a decrease in the terminal glycolytic products pyruvate and lactate as well as significant depletion of the glucose-derived metabolites glycerol-3-phosphate and 2-hydroxyglutarate (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3A,B).

claim: TRIM32 is required for sustaining the conversion of glucose to pyruvate and lactate in L3 larvae.
source: These metabolic changes suggest that TRIM32 is required for sustaining the conversion of glucose to pyruvate and lactate in L3 larvae.
evidence: The claim is inferred from metabolomics data showing decreased pyruvate and lactate levels.

claim: Wild-type body wall muscles undergo dramatic growth from L2 to L3 stage.
source: One larval tissue that requires high glycolytic activity is the somatic musculature, where WT body wall muscles undergo dramatic growth as development proceeds from second instar larvae (L2) (Figure 3C,G) to the L3 stage (Figure 3D,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data (Figure 3C,D,G).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 results in reduced muscle diameter in both L2 and L3 larvae.
source: While multiple independent alleles of tn have been shown to produce smaller muscles (Domsch et al., 2013; LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012), quantification of tn-/- confirmed a decrease in larval muscle diameter in both L2 (Figure 3E,G) and L3 individuals (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data (Figure 3E,F,G) and citations to published literature (Domsch et al., 2013; LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 compromises the glycolytic-driven growth of muscles during larval development.
source: Thus, loss of TRIM32 compromises the glycolytic-driven growth of muscles during larval development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing reduced muscle size and decreased glycolytic activity in tn mutants.

claim: Loss of TRIM32 results in reduced extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) in muscle carcasses.
source: Since a major contributor to extracellular acidification is lactate excretion into medium during glycolysis (Mookerjee and Brand, 2015; TeSlaa and Teitell, 2014), we anticipated, and indeed, observed a reduction in ECAR upon loss of TRIM32 (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse XFe96 Analyzer data (Figure 3H) and citations to published literature (Mookerjee and Brand, 2015; TeSlaa and Teitell, 2014).

claim: Glycolytic metabolism produces fewer protons in tn-/- muscle carcasses compared to wild-type controls.
source: Our analysis revealed that glycolytic metabolism produces fewer protons in tn-/- muscle carcasses as compared with WT controls (Figure 3I), thus supporting our hypothesis that TRIM32 is required to support glycolytic flux.
evidence: The claim is supported by proton efflux rate (PER) assay data (Figure 3I).

claim: Wild-type muscles show a markedly shorter NADH fluorescent lifetime than tn-/- muscles.
source: This analysis revealed that WT muscles analyzed by FLIM showed a markedly shorter lifetime than tn-/- muscles (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) data (Figure 3J).

claim: Free, unbound NADH is predominant in highly glycolytic cells.
source: Since free, unbound NADH is predominate in highly glycolytic cells, here we confirm a reduction in the glycolytic profile upon loss of TRIM32.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about NADH states in glycolytic cells.

claim: TRIM32-mediated regulation of glycolysis in muscle tissue is cell autonomous.
source: Here, we conclude that TRIM32-mediated regulation of glycolysis in muscle tissue is cell autonomous.
evidence: The claim is inferred from tissue-specific RNAi experiments showing that knockdown of TRIM32 in muscle, but not neurons, reduces lactate levels (Figure 4E).

claim: Muscle-specific expression of TRIM32 in a tn-/- background restores muscle diameter to wild-type levels.
source: As a positive control, we expressed a cDNA encoding for TRIM32 in tn-/- muscle tissue (tn-/-; mef >TRIM32) and found that the muscle diameter was restored to WT (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data (Figure 4F).

claim: Overexpression of ERR in tn-/- muscles improves muscle size.
source: Overexpression of ERR in tn-/- muscles not only improved muscle size (Figure 4F), but also corrected the functional deficit associated with the inability of tn-/- to contract body wall muscles during pupal morphogenesis (Figure 4G,H; Domsch et al., 2013; LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data (Figure 4F) and citations to published literature (Domsch et al., 2013; LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).

claim: Overexpression of ERR in tn-/- muscles corrects the functional deficit in muscle contraction during pupal morphogenesis.
source: Overexpression of ERR in tn-/- muscles not only improved muscle size (Figure 4F), but also corrected the functional deficit associated with the inability of tn-/- to contract body wall muscles during pupal morphogenesis (Figure 4G,H; Domsch et al., 2013; LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by pupal morphology data (Figure 4G,H) and citations to published literature (Domsch et al., 2013; LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).

claim: Protein levels of Ald and Pglym are stabilized upon expression of ERR in tn-/- muscles.
source: Importantly, protein levels of Ald and Pglym were stabilized upon expression of ERR in tn-/- muscles (Figure 4I,J), indicating that restoration of glycolytic protein levels is sufficient to recover TRIM32-mediated growth defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data (Figure 4I,J).

claim: Restoration of glycolytic protein levels is sufficient to recover TRIM32-mediated growth defects.
source: Importantly, protein levels of Ald and Pglym were stabilized upon expression of ERR in tn-/- muscles (Figure 4I,J), indicating that restoration of glycolytic protein levels is sufficient to recover TRIM32-mediated growth defects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that ERR expression restores glycolytic protein levels and rescues muscle growth defects.

claim: Loss of TRIM32 induces a significant decrease in eleven of the twenty amino acids in L3 larvae.
source: Our metabolomics analysis revealed that loss of TRIM32 not only disrupts the production of glycolytic intermediates, but also induces a significant decrease in eleven of the twenty amino acids (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data (Figure 5A).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 results in a >1.5 fold decrease in serine and glycine levels.
source: These changes in amino acid abundance are likely due to both decreased synthesis and increased catabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), as we observed that tn-/- exhibited a>1.5 decrease in not only serine and glycine levels which are normally synthesized from glucose, but also a reduction in the anaplerotic amino acids proline and aspartic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 results in a reduction in the anaplerotic amino acids proline and aspartic acid.
source: These changes in amino acid abundance are likely due to both decreased synthesis and increased catabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), as we observed that tn-/- exhibited a>1.5 decrease in not only serine and glycine levels which are normally synthesized from glucose, but also a reduction in the anaplerotic amino acids proline and aspartic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 induces a significant depletion of alanine.
source: Moreover, loss of TRIM32 also induced a significant depletion of alanine, which is both synthesized from and catabolized into pyruvate.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: tn-/- mutant larvae fed a diet consisting of yeast extract exhibit no decrease in muscle diameter compared to wild-type.
source: In contrast, mutant larvae fed a diet consisting of only yeast extract or supplemented with all 20 amino acids exhibited no decrease in muscle diameter (Figure 5D,E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data (Figure 5D,E,F).

claim: tn-/- mutant larvae fed a diet supplemented with all 20 amino acids exhibit no decrease in muscle diameter compared to wild-type.
source: In contrast, mutant larvae fed a diet consisting of only yeast extract or supplemented with all 20 amino acids exhibited no decrease in muscle diameter (Figure 5D,E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data (Figure 5D,E,F).

claim: Supplementation of the larval diet with yeast extract or amino acids suppresses body mass and muscle contraction phenotypes in tn-/- mutants.
source: Supplementation of the larval diet with yeast extract or amino acids, however, suppressed both phenotypes in tn-/- (Figure 5G,H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by body mass and pupal morphology data (Figure 5G,H,I).

claim: tn-/- mutants are uniquely sensitive to dietary amino acids.
source: These results suggest that tn-/- mutants are uniquely sensitive to dietary amino acids, consistent with the smaller amino acid pool size observed upon loss of TRIM32.
evidence: The claim is inferred from dietary supplementation experiments showing rescue of phenotypes with amino acids.

claim: Loss of TRIM32 reduces the average area of the larval brain by approximately 40%.
source: The overall size of larval brains dissected from WT (Figure 6A) or tn-/- (Figure 6B) L3 individuals showed a dramatic size difference, whereby loss of TRIM32 reduced the average area of the larval brain by ~40% (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data (Figure 6A,B,G).

claim: Reduced larval brain size upon loss of TRIM32 is cell autonomous.
source: To determine if a brain-specific reduction in TRIM32 is cell autonomous, we induced two independent tn RNAi lines in both neuronal (elav >tn RNAi) and muscle tissue (mef2 >tn RNAi). As expected, reduced larval brain size was observed upon RNAi knockdown of TRIM32 with elav-Gal4 (Figure 6C,D,G), but not with the mef2 driver (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue-specific RNAi experiments (Figure 6C,D,E,F,G).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 in isolated L3 larval brains shows a reduced glycolytic rate.
source: PER analysis (Neville et al., 2018) of individual larval brains isolated from tn-/- showed a reduced glycolytic rate compared to their WT counterparts (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by proton efflux rate (PER) assay data (Figure 6H) and citation to published literature (Neville et al., 2018).

claim: L-lactate levels are lower in dissected tn-/- larval brains compared to wild-type.
source: Consistent with reduced substrate flux through the glycolytic pathway, L-lactate levels were also lower in dissected tn-/- larval brains (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by L-lactate assay data (Figure 6I).

claim: Decreased lactate levels in larval brains result from inducing tn RNAi in neuronal, but not muscle tissue.
source: Tissue-specific knockdown experiments verified that decreased lactate levels in larval brains resulted from inducing tn RNAi in neuronal, but not muscle tissue (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue-specific RNAi experiments (Figure 6I).

claim: Defective cell proliferation does not account for the overall brain size reduction in tn-/- mutants.
source: Defective cell proliferation (assayed by EdU incorporation) or increased cell death (assessed using TUNEL labeling and cleaved-Caspase3 immunoreactivity) did not account for the overall brain size reduction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation, TUNEL, and cleaved-Caspase3 data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–I).

claim: Increased cell death does not account for the overall brain size reduction in tn-/- mutants.
source: Defective cell proliferation (assayed by EdU incorporation) or increased cell death (assessed using TUNEL labeling and cleaved-Caspase3 immunoreactivity) did not account for the overall brain size reduction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL and cleaved-Caspase3 data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–I).

claim: Individual brain cell size is markedly reduced upon loss of TRIM32.
source: Quantitation of individual brain cell size revealed a marked reduction upon loss of TRIM32 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J–M) consistent with an increase in cell size as the primary mechanism for TRIM32-mediated tissue growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell size quantitation data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J–M).

claim: An increase in cell size is the primary mechanism for TRIM32-mediated tissue growth in larval brains.
source: Quantitation of individual brain cell size revealed a marked reduction upon loss of TRIM32 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J–M) consistent with an increase in cell size as the primary mechanism for TRIM32-mediated tissue growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing reduced cell size but no change in proliferation or cell death.

claim: Neither LDH activity nor LDH-GFP expression are detectable in control wing discs.
source: Unlike muscle or brain tissue, neither LDH activity (Wang et al., 2016) nor LDH-GFP expression (Figure 7A) were detectable in control wing discs, suggesting that this tissue does not exhibit elevated glycolytic activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by LDH-GFP expression data (Figure 7A) and citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 does not alter the volume of wing discs compared to wild-type control discs.
source: Accordingly, loss of TRIM32 did not alter the volume (Figure 7D) or area (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C) of mutant discs compared to WT control discs.
evidence: The claim is supported by wing disc volume data (Figure 7D).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 does not alter the area of wing discs compared to wild-type control discs.
source: Accordingly, loss of TRIM32 did not alter the volume (Figure 7D) or area (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C) of mutant discs compared to WT control discs.
evidence: The claim is supported by wing disc area data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).

claim: TRIM32-deficient wing discs do not show altered glycolytic activity as measured by PER assays.
source: Moreover, measurements of glycolytic flux using either PER assays (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) or FILM analysis confirmed that TRIM32-deficient wing discs (Figure 7F,G) did not show altered glycolytic activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).

claim: TRIM32-deficient wing discs do not show altered glycolytic activity as measured by FLIM analysis.
source: Moreover, measurements of glycolytic flux using either PER assays (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) or FILM analysis confirmed that TRIM32-deficient wing discs (Figure 7F,G) did not show altered glycolytic activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data (Figure 7F,G).

claim: Overexpression of activated Pvr receptor (Pvract) in dpp-expressing wing disc cells increases LDH-GFP expression.
source: To examine the possibility that TRIM32 regulates the growth of highly glycolytic tumor cells, we confirmed that overexpression of the activated platelet PDGF/VEGF receptor (Pvract) in dpp-expressing wing disc cells increased LDH-GFP expression and promoted tissue overgrowth (Figure 7B,D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by LDH-GFP expression data (Figure 7B) and citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Overexpression of activated Pvr receptor (Pvract) in dpp-expressing wing disc cells promotes tissue overgrowth.
source: To examine the possibility that TRIM32 regulates the growth of highly glycolytic tumor cells, we confirmed that overexpression of the activated platelet PDGF/VEGF receptor (Pvract) in dpp-expressing wing disc cells increased LDH-GFP expression and promoted tissue overgrowth (Figure 7B,D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing disc volume data (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) and citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Removal of TRIM32 causes smaller tumors in wing discs overexpressing Pvract.
source: Remarkably, removal of TRIM32 caused smaller tumors, effectively reducing the overall size of the wing disc (Figure 7C,D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing disc volume data (Figure 7C,D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Approximately 50% of TRIM32-deficient wing discs lost LDH-GFP expression in Pvract-induced tumors.
source: Analysis of LDH-GFP expression revealed biological variability as ~50% of TRIM32-deficient wing discs lost LDH-GFP expression (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by LDH-GFP expression analysis (Figure 7E).

claim: FLIM analysis shows a decrease in the glycolytic activity of tumors grown in tn-/- larvae compared to Pvr-induced tumors in wild-type individuals.
source: FILM analysis validated a decrease in the glycolytic activity of tumors grown in tn-/- larvae compared to Pvr-induced tumors in WT individuals (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM data (Figure 7F,G).

claim: TRIM32 is required for cell growth in both normal and tumorous glycolytic tissues.
source: Collectively, our data show that TRIM32 is required for cell growth in both normal and tumorous glycolytic tissues, thus providing a novel molecular explanation for the upregulation of TRIM32 in multiple types of cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing TRIM32 requirement in muscle, brain, and tumor growth.

claim: TRIM32 directly interacts with and maintains the levels of two glycolytic enzymes, Aldolase and Phosphoglycerate mutase.
source: We show here that TRIM32 directly interacts with and maintains the levels of two glycolytic enzymes.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assays, co-immunoprecipitation, and Western blot data.

claim: Decreased protein levels of Ald and Pglym cripple glycolytic flux, blunting the generation of metabolic intermediates that contribute to anabolic synthesis necessary to sustain cell growth.
source: Decreased protein levels of both Ald and Pglym (and possibly other glycolytic enzymes) cripple this rapid flux, effectively blunting the generation of metabolic intermediates that contribute to anabolic synthesis necessary to sustain cell growth (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing reduced glycolytic enzyme levels, reduced glycolytic flux, and reduced cell growth.

claim: The overall body size of tn mutant pupae is not smaller than wild-type counterparts under starvation conditions.
source: First, the overall body size of tn mutant pupae is not smaller than their WT counterparts under starvation conditions, but instead elongated due to defective muscle contraction (Domsch et al., 2013; LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012; Figure 4G,H; Figure 5H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by pupal morphology data (Figure 4G,H; Figure 5H,I) and citations to published literature (Domsch et al., 2013; LaBeau-DiMenna et al., 2012).

claim: The size of the wing disc is not altered upon loss of TRIM32.
source: Second, the size of the wing disc and midgut, both tissues that show reduced growth in poorly fed larvae, is not altered upon loss of TRIM32 (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C; Figure 7—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing disc size data (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).

claim: The size of the midgut is not altered upon loss of TRIM32.
source: Second, the size of the wing disc and midgut, both tissues that show reduced growth in poorly fed larvae, is not altered upon loss of TRIM32 (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C; Figure 7—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by midgut size data (Figure 7—figure supplement 2F–H).

claim: Cellular glucose uptake is normal in tn-/- larval brains and wing disc-derived tumors.
source: Surprisingly, cellular glucose uptake assayed by the non-metabolizable fluorescent glucose analog 2-[N-(7-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-4-yl)amino]−2-deoxyglucose (2-NBDG), was normal in tn-/- larval brains and wing disc-derived tumors (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–D), demonstrating that glucose is not a limiting substrate for glycolysis in isolated tn-/- tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-NBDG uptake assay data (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–D).

claim: Food intake remains constant upon tissue-specific knockdown of TRIM32 in muscle or brains that show reduced tissue growth.
source: Finally, even though systemic effects compromise feeding in tn-/- whole larvae (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E), food intake remained constant upon tissue-specific knockdown of TRIM32 in muscle or brains that show reduced tissue growth (Figure 7—figure supplement 2I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by food intake assay data (Figure 7—figure supplement 2I,J).

claim: TRIM32 functions in a cell autonomous manner to regulate tissue growth, independent of systemic nutritional status.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that TRIM32 functions in a cell autonomous manner to regulate tissue growth, independent of systemic nutritional status.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing tissue-specific effects and normal glucose uptake.

claim: Loss of TRIM32 decreases both lactate and glycerol-3-phosphate levels, mimicking the reduced carbohydrate metabolism in Ldh, Gpdh1 double mutants.
source: Our results show that loss of TRIM32 decreases both lactate and glycerol-3-phosphate levels (Figure 3A,B), thus mimicking the reduced carbohydrate metabolism in Ldh, Gpdh1 double mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3A,B) and comparison to published findings on Ldh, Gpdh1 double mutants.

claim: TRIM32 is upregulated in proliferating satellite cells.
source: TRIM32 is upregulated in proliferating satellite cells and loss of this protein prevents myotube regeneration, partially through the misregulation of NDRG and c-Myc (Kudryashova et al., 2012; Mokhonova et al., 2015; Nicklas et al., 2012; Servián-Morilla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kudryashova et al., 2012; Mokhonova et al., 2015; Nicklas et al., 2012; Servián-Morilla et al., 2019).

claim: Loss of TRIM32 prevents myotube regeneration, partially through the misregulation of NDRG and c-Myc.
source: TRIM32 is upregulated in proliferating satellite cells and loss of this protein prevents myotube regeneration, partially through the misregulation of NDRG and c-Myc (Kudryashova et al., 2012; Mokhonova et al., 2015; Nicklas et al., 2012; Servián-Morilla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kudryashova et al., 2012; Mokhonova et al., 2015; Nicklas et al., 2012; Servián-Morilla et al., 2019).

claim: TRIM32-mediated deregulation of actin, α-actinin, tropomyosin, and desmin contributes to muscle atrophy.
source: TRIM32-mediated deregulation of key muscle substrates, including actin, α-actinin, tropomyosin, and desmin, contribute to muscle atrophy (Cohen et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2012; Kudryashova et al., 2005; Locke et al., 2009), but studies have not been performed to directly test this model in the context of LGMD2H.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cohen et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2012; Kudryashova et al., 2005; Locke et al., 2009).

claim: Mammalian glycolytic type II fibers are preferentially affected over oxidative type I fibers in muscle atrophy induced by aging/starvation and in Duchenne's and Becker muscular dystrophies.
source: Interestingly, mammalian glycolytic type II fibers are preferentially affected over oxidative type I fibers in muscle atrophy induced by aging/starvation, as well as in Duchenne's and Becker muscular dystrophies (DMD) (Ciciliot et al., 2013; Pant et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ciciliot et al., 2013; Pant et al., 2015).

claim: TRIM32 KO muscles show a decrease in the glycolytic proteins GAPDH and PyK.
source: TRIM32 KO muscles also show a decrease in the glycolytic proteins GAPDH and PyK (Mokhonova et al., 2015), just as we observe a reduction in Ald and Pglym levels in tn-/- muscles, suggesting that TRIM32-mediated regulation of glycolysis may be a general mechanism that underlies some muscular dystrophies.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Mokhonova et al., 2015).

claim: TRIM32-mediated regulation of glycolysis may be a general mechanism that underlies some muscular dystrophies.
source: TRIM32 KO muscles also show a decrease in the glycolytic proteins GAPDH and PyK (Mokhonova et al., 2015), just as we observe a reduction in Ald and Pglym levels in tn-/- muscles, suggesting that TRIM32-mediated regulation of glycolysis may be a general mechanism that underlies some muscular dystrophies.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on comparison of findings in TRIM32 KO muscles and tn-/- muscles.

claim: Piasy, p53 and Abi2 are known targets of TRIM32 E3 activity that regulate the proliferative balance in cancer cells.
source: Piasy, p53 and Abi2 are known targets of TRIM32 E3 activity that regulate the proliferative balance in cancer cells (Albor et al., 2006; Kano et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Albor et al., 2006; Kano et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014).

claim: The NHL domain of TRIM32 may serve as a scaffold for the subcellular localization of glycolytic proteins to limit diffusion of substrates during glycolysis.
source: Another possibility, which we favor, is that the NHL domain of TRIM32 serves as a scaffold for the subcellular localization of glycolytic proteins to limit diffusion of substrates during glycolysis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, representing a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Drosophila larval development is preceded by a metabolic switch that induces the coordinate upregulation of genes involved in glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and lactate dehydrogenase.
source: This observation is particularly apparent in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, where the onset of larval development is preceded by a metabolic switch that induces the coordinate upregulation of genes involved in glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (Tennessen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tennessen et al., 2011).

claim: The metabolic program in Drosophila larvae allows larvae to use dietary carbohydrates for both energy production and biomass accumulation.
source: The resulting metabolic program allows larvae to use dietary carbohydrates for both energy production and biomass accumulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the metabolic switch described in Tennessen et al., 2011.

claim: The metabolic transition to glycolysis is essential for muscle growth and development in Drosophila larval muscles.
source: Moreover, studies of Drosophila larval muscles reveal that this metabolic transition is essential for muscle growth and development, suggesting that glycolysis serves a key role in controlling growth (Tennessen et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tennessen et al., 2014b).

claim: Drosophila larval muscle increases in size without cell divisions.
source: Moreover, since larval muscle increases in size without cell divisions, larval muscle provides an unusual opportunity to understand how glycolytic metabolism promotes growth independent of cell division.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila larval muscle development.

claim: TRIM32 protein levels are upregulated in multiple tumor types.
source: Importantly, TRIM32 protein levels are upregulated in multiple tumor types, suggesting that TRIM32 is a key player in growth regulation (Horn et al., 2004; Ito et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Horn et al., 2004; Ito et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2018).

claim: Two other Drosophila NHL-containing proteins, Brat and Mei-P26, act as tumor suppressors in the larval brain and female germline, respectively.
source: There is precedence for NHL function in controlling cell proliferation as two other Drosophila NHL-containing proteins, Brat and Mei-P26, act as tumor suppressors in the larval brain and female germline, respectively (Arama et al., 2000; Edwards et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Arama et al., 2000; Edwards et al., 2003).

claim: TRIM32 promotes glucose metabolism through the stabilization of glycolytic enzyme levels.
source: Our data show that TRIM32 promotes glucose metabolism through the stabilization of glycolytic enzyme levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing TRIM32 interactions with glycolytic enzymes and reduced enzyme levels in tn mutants.

claim: Increased rate of TRIM32-mediated glycolytic flux generates precursors that are utilized for biomass production.
source: This increased rate of TRIM32-mediated glycolytic flux generates precursors that are utilized for biomass production.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing increased glycolytic flux and cell growth in the presence of TRIM32.

claim: The TRIM32 mechanism operates in both non-dividing muscle cells and proliferating larval brain cells.
source: Surprisingly, this mechanism operates in both non-dividing muscle cells as well as in proliferating larval brain cells, demonstrating a universal metabolic function for TRIM32 in growth control.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing TRIM32 effects in both muscle and brain tissues.

claim: Loss of Drosophila TRIM32 shows reduced levels of glycolytic intermediates and amino acids.
source: Loss of Drosophila TRIM32, encoded by thin (tn), shows reduced levels of glycolytic intermediates and amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: The altered metabolic profile in tn mutants correlates with a reduction in the size of glycolytic larval muscle and brain tissue.
source: This altered metabolic profile correlates with a reduction in the size of glycolytic larval muscle and brain tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics and microscopy data.

claim: Dietary amino acid supplementation in tn mutants improves muscle mass.
source: Consistent with a role for metabolic intermediates in glycolysis-driven biomass production, dietary amino acid supplementation in tn mutants improves muscle mass.
evidence: The claim is supported by dietary supplementation experiments.

claim: TRIM32 is required for ectopic growth in a wing disc-associated tumor model.
source: Remarkably, TRIM32 is also required for ectopic growth - loss of TRIM32 in a wing disc-associated tumor model reduces glycolytic metabolism and restricts growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor growth and glycolytic flux data in wing disc tumors.

claim: Loss of TRIM32 in a wing disc-associated tumor model reduces glycolytic metabolism.
source: Remarkably, TRIM32 is also required for ectopic growth - loss of TRIM32 in a wing disc-associated tumor model reduces glycolytic metabolism and restricts growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by FLIM and PER data in wing disc tumors.
